art.description: Jesus touches his own lips as he faces the mute man, who begins to speak.
art.significance: Tissot illustrates the healing that ends Matthew 9.
art.symbolism: The man's restored speech is answered by the crowd's wonder and the Pharisees' accusation.
art.impact: Part of Tissot's series of healing scenes.

events.title: The last visit to Nazareth
events.summary: Jesus returns with his disciples to his own country and teaches in the synagogue on the Sabbath. The people are astonished but take offense: is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, whose brothers and sisters live among them? Jesus says a prophet is not without honor except in his own country. He could do no mighty work there, except heal a few sick people, and he marveled at their unbelief.
events.journey: About 28 miles from Capernaum up through the Arbel pass to Nazareth.

scripture.text: Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon, and are not his sisters here with us?" And they took offense at him.
And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands upon a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled because of their unbelief. And he went about among the villages teaching.

art.title: View of Nazareth
art.medium: Drawing on paper
art.description: The small hill town of Nazareth seen across its valley.
art.significance: A landscape study made during Tissot's Holy Land travels.
art.symbolism: The modest town where Jesus grew up and where he was not honored.
art.impact: Records Nazareth as it looked in the 1880s, before modern growth.

events.orderNote: Robertson sees no reason to identify this with the visit in Luke 4:16–30 (§39): that was at the start of the ministry, this near its close, and the details differ. Many scholars take them as one visit.

Mt.text: And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.

Mk.text: And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands upon a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled because of their unbelief.

events.title: The Twelve sent out two by two
events.summary: Seeing the crowds harassed and helpless like sheep without a shepherd, Jesus sends out the Twelve two by two with authority over unclean spirits. They are to preach that the kingdom of heaven is at hand, heal the sick, take no money or bag, and stay in whatever house welcomes them. He warns them of persecution: he sends them as sheep among wolves. They go out preaching repentance, casting out demons and anointing the sick with oil, while Jesus himself tours the villages.
events.journey: A third circuit of the villages of Galilee, while the Twelve go out in pairs.

scripture.text: And preach as you go, saying, 'The kingdom of heaven is at hand.' Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without pay, give without pay.
"Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.
So they went out and preached that men should repent. And they cast out many demons, and anointed with oil many that were sick and healed them.

echoes.note: Moses prays that God's people may not be "as sheep which have no shepherd."

art.title: The Exhortation to the Apostles
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Seated under a tree, Jesus speaks to the Twelve gathered on the ground around him.
art.significance: Tissot illustrates the mission discourse of Matthew 10.
art.symbolism: The close circle of listeners is about to be scattered two by two.
art.impact: Part of Tissot's series on the training of the Twelve.

art.title: On Entering the House, Salute It
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: An apostle stands in an open doorway and touches his forehead in greeting, a companion behind him.
art.significance: Tissot illustrates one instruction from the mission charge.
art.symbolism: The greeting of peace is the apostles' first gift to each household.
art.impact: Shows the Gospel's instructions as everyday actions.

events.orderNote: Matthew gathers into this charge sayings about persecution that Mark and Luke place later (e.g. Mark 13:9–13). Robertson counts this as the third tour of Galilee.

Mt.text: These twelve Jesus sent out, charging them, "Go nowhere among the Gentiles, and enter no town of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

Mk.text: And he called to him the twelve, and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits.

Lk.text: and he sent them out to preach the kingdom of God and to heal.

events.title: Herod Antipas hears of Jesus
events.summary: News of Jesus and of the mighty works done by the Twelve reaches Herod Antipas. Some say John the Baptist has been raised from the dead, others that Jesus is Elijah or one of the prophets. Herod, haunted by his guilt, says, "John, whom I beheaded, has been raised." Luke adds that he sought to see Jesus, a wish fulfilled only at the trial.
events.stay: Antipas ruled from his new capital at Tiberias.

scripture.text: King Herod heard of it; for Jesus' name had become known. Some said, "John the baptizer has been raised from the dead; that is why these powers are at work in him."
But when Herod heard of it he said, "John, whom I beheaded, has been raised."
Herod said, "John I beheaded; but who is this about whom I hear such things?" And he sought to see him.

art.title: Herod
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Herod Antipas, in rich robes and a tall headdress, stands with folded arms and a hard stare.
art.significance: Tissot gives the tetrarch a portrait of his own, as a figure of worldly power.
art.symbolism: His guarded, suspicious look fits the guilty fear of Mark 6:16.
art.impact: Part of Tissot's gallery of Gospel characters.

events.orderNote: Robertson places Herod in Tiberias; the Gospels do not say where he was. Jesus soon withdraws beyond Antipas' territory, partly, Robertson thinks, to avoid his jealousy.

Mt.text: and he said to his servants, "This is John the Baptist, he has been raised from the dead; that is why these powers are at work in him."

Mk.text: But when Herod heard of it he said, "John, whom I beheaded, has been raised."

Lk.text: Herod said, "John I beheaded; but who is this about whom I hear such things?" And he sought to see him.

events.title: The beheading of John the Baptist
people: The daughter of Herodias (Salome, per Josephus)
events.summary: Mark tells the story in flashback. Herod had arrested John because John told him it was not lawful to have his brother's wife, Herodias. Herod feared John as a holy man and liked to hear him, but Herodias wanted him dead. At Herod's birthday banquet her daughter dances and pleases him, and he swears to give her whatever she asks. Prompted by her mother, she asks for John's head on a platter, and the king, though sorry, sends a guard to behead him in prison. John's disciples take his body and bury it, then go and tell Jesus.
events.stay: John was held in prison, at Machaerus according to Josephus, for some months before his death.

scripture.text: For John said to Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife."
And she came in immediately with haste to the king, and asked, saying, "I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter."

And immediately the king sent a soldier of the guard and gave orders to bring his head. He went and beheaded him in the prison, and brought his head on a platter, and gave it to the girl; and the girl gave it to her mother.

echoes.note: Queen Jezebel vows to kill the prophet Elijah, as Herodias seeks John's life.
"It shall be given you, even to the half of my kingdom."

art.title: The Beheading of Saint John the Baptist
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.location: Oratory of St John's Co-Cathedral, Valletta, Malta
art.description: In a prison courtyard the executioner kneels over John's body and draws a knife, while a young woman holds out a golden platter and two prisoners watch through a barred window.
art.significance: Caravaggio's largest painting and the only one he signed, in the blood flowing from John's neck.
art.symbolism: The vast empty wall and dim light make the killing feel bleak and ordinary; the prisoners at the window are witnesses for us.
art.impact: Painted for the Knights of Malta while Caravaggio was a member of the order; it is considered one of the masterpieces of Western painting.

art.title: The Daughter of Herodias Dancing
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Herodias' daughter bends backward in an acrobatic dance on the banquet table before Herod and his guests, while harpists play below and armed guards stand by.
art.significance: Tissot imagines the court of Antipas from his study of Eastern palaces and dress.
art.symbolism: The dance that pleases the king leads to the oath and John's death.
art.impact: One of the most striking images in Tissot's series, often reproduced.

events.orderNote: Mark places the story as a flashback; John probably died some time before Herod heard of the Twelve's mission. Josephus (Antiquities 18.5.2) names Machaerus and says Herod killed John fearing an uprising; he names Herodias' daughter as Salome. Some think the banquet was held at Tiberias, though the head was then brought from Machaerus, a long way off.

Mt.text: And his disciples came and took the body and buried it; and they went and told Jesus.

Mk.text: for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and kept him safe. When he heard him, he was much perplexed; and yet he heard him gladly.
